a: Happy are the blameless in their way
t: An alphabet in groups of eight
p: Every verse of a stanza begins with the same Hebrew letter: eight verses for each of the 22 letters.
b: Psalm 119 is the longest alphabet poem (acrostic) in the Bible and the longest chapter. It has 22 stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and each stanza has eight verses. All eight verses of the first stanza begin with alef (here ashrei, "happy"), all eight of the second with bet, and so on to tav: 22 × 8 = 176 verses. The section headings name each letter; the KJV prints them as ALEPH, BETH, GIMEL. English cannot keep the pattern, so the Plain keeps the opening word in front where it can ("And" in 119:41–48, "Good" in 119:65–72, "Forever" in 119:89). The psalm has no title, so its Hebrew and English verse numbers are the same. In the Greek and Latin it is Psalm 118, the number used in Catholic and Orthodox prayer books and in the church fathers.
orig: אַשְׁרֵי (ashrei), first word of the alef stanza
r: Psalm 9:1–20; Psalm 25:1–22; Psalm 34:1–22; Psalm 37:1–40; Psalm 111:1–10; Psalm 145:1–21; Proverbs 31:10–31; Lamentations 1:1–22

a: Happy
t: The same first word as Psalm 1
p: Psalm 119 opens like Psalm 1: "Happy" are those who walk by the LORD's law.
b: Psalm 1 begins "Happy is the person" and makes the law of the LORD that person's delight (1:1–2). Psalm 119 opens with the same word, ashrei, and the same picture of walking a road (see the note at 1:1 on "Happy" rather than "blessed"). Psalms 1, 19 and 119 are often called the torah psalms. Many scholars think the editors set Psalm 1 at the door of the Psalter and Psalm 119 near its end so that the whole book would be read as instruction to be studied, not only songs to be sung.

a: the LORD's law
p: The psalm names God's teaching with eight words, and nearly every verse uses at least one.
b: The poet rings changes on eight nouns: torah "law" (25 times), 'edot/'edwot "decrees" (23), piqqudim "orders" (21), chuqqim "rules" (22), mitsvot "commands" (22), mishpatim "rulings" (23, including three uses in other senses), davar "word" (24) and 'imrah "saying" (19), counting by the Hebrew word list. The Plain gives each word one English rendering all the way through, so a reader can follow them (the table is on the chapter page). Scholars disagree on how different they are. Some think each keeps its own shade; most think they work as near-synonyms, eight names for the one teaching of God, in the way the stanzas have eight lines. Torah means "instruction, teaching" before it means a law code (see the note at 1:2).

a: his decrees
p: 'Edot is the covenant's terms as solemnly attested. The KJV says "testimonies".
b: The word comes from 'ed, "witness". The tablets of the Ten Words are "the tablets of the 'edut" and the ark is "the ark of the 'edut" (Exodus 25:16; Exodus 31:18). So the KJV "testimonies" is literal: these are the terms God bound himself and Israel to, with witnesses. The Psalms on this site render it "decree" (19:7; 78:5); Exodus keeps "the testimony" for the tablets in the ark. The Hebrew of Psalm 119 has two spellings, 'edot and 'edwot, which may come from two related nouns; the Plain makes no difference between them.

a: Yes, they do nothing unjust
t: A verse without a law word
p: Verse 3 is one of a handful in the psalm with none of the eight words for God's teaching.
b: An old claim, often repeated, is that every verse but one names God's word. Counted strictly by the eight nouns, four verses have none: 119:3, 119:37, 119:90 and 119:122. Verses 3 and 37 have "way(s)" (derekh) and 90 has "faithfulness" ('emunah), which some count as extra law words; only 122 has nothing like them. In 119:132 mishpat means "what is right, the custom", not a ruling, so some also count it as empty. Scholars read the gaps either as signs that the text has slipped in copying (see the variant at 119:37) or as the poet's freedom: the pattern is strong but not mechanical.

a: in his ways they walk
p: The Greek reads "those who do lawless things have not walked in his ways".
b: Rahlfs' Greek text (checked on bibelkommentare.de) and Codex Sinaiticus (checked in the Lake facsimile as transcribed on sourcelibrary.org) both read ou gar hoi ergazomenoi tēn anomian en tais hodois autou eporeuthēsan, "for those who work lawlessness have not walked in his ways". The Hebrew praises the blameless; the Greek warns about their opposite. The Greek translator may have read the Hebrew lines as one sentence. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: your orders
p: Piqqudim, from paqad "to appoint, to put in charge", is found only in the Psalms.
b: Piqqudim comes from the verb for an officer or overseer who assigns duties and checks on them (Genesis 39:4–5; Numbers 3:10). It occurs only in the Psalms: 19:8, 103:18, 111:7 and 21 times in Psalm 119. The site renders it "orders" everywhere (19:8). The KJV and most modern versions say "precepts", a Latin word for the same thing. The Greek usually translates it with entolai, "commandments", the same word it uses for mitsvot, so in the Greek and Latin two of the eight words become one.

a: your rules
p: Chuqqim are fixed rules. The root means "to cut, engrave".
b: The verb chaqaq means to carve or inscribe (Isaiah 22:16; Isaiah 49:16), so a choq is something set down and fixed, a standing rule or limit. The site renders it "rules" in every book, alongside mishpatim "rulings" (18:22; 89:30–31; Deuteronomy 4:1). Psalm 119:16 uses the feminine form chuqqot, also "rules". The prayer "teach me your rules" comes six times (119:12, 26, 64, 68, 124, 135), and 119:171 praises God for doing it.

a: the rulings of your righteousness
p: Mishpatim are a judge's verdicts. "The rulings of your righteousness" comes five times.
b: Mishpat is what a shofet, a judge, hands down: a decision in a case, and so a precedent, a ruling that settles how things are done (Exodus 21:1). "The rulings of your righteousness" (119:7, 62, 106, 160, 164) means rulings that come from God's own rightness. The word can also mean "justice" in general (119:121), "judgment" on enemies (119:84) or the custom, what is right, in 119:132; the Plain changes the English there and says so.

a: How will a young man make his path clean?
t: A teacher and a young man
p: The bet stanza sounds like a school: how does a young man stay clean? By God's word.
b: The question and answer recall Proverbs, where a father or teacher instructs "my son" (Proverbs 1:8; Proverbs 4:10–13). Many scholars think Psalm 119 came out of the circles that taught the law to young Jews after the exile, the world of scribes like Ezra (Ezra 7:10) and of Ben Sira's school (Sirach 51:23). Others read verse 9 as the speaker asking about himself: he calls himself "small" in 119:141, and old men appear as the ones he outstrips (119:100). Christian youth ministries quote it often.

a: as your word says
p: Davar is "word"; 'imrah is "saying". English Bibles often call both "word" or "promise".
b: Davar (24 times) is the ordinary word for a spoken word or a matter. 'Imrah (19 times) comes from 'amar, "to say", and is a more poetic word: "what you have said". In many verses it means a promise (119:38, 41, 50, 76, 116), and modern versions often translate it "promise". The Plain keeps "saying" everywhere, as the site does at 12:6 ("The LORD's sayings"), so that the reader can see which word is used. The Greek mostly keeps them apart: logos for davar, logion for 'imrah.

a: In my heart I have treasured your saying
p: Tsafan means to hide something valuable. The picture is learning by heart.
b: The verb is used for hiding treasure or saving up stores (Proverbs 2:1; Proverbs 2:7; Proverbs 7:1). To "treasure" God's saying in the heart is to know it so well that it is there when temptation comes: Deuteronomy 6:6 tells Israel to keep God's words "on your heart". This verse has become a motto for memorizing Scripture, in Jewish learning and in Christian Sunday schools alike. Jesus answering the tempter with Deuteronomy (Matthew 4:1–11) is often given as the example.

a: Blessed are you, LORD
t: The first words of every Jewish blessing
p: Barukh attah YHWH, "Blessed are you, LORD", opens every berakhah in Jewish prayer.
b: This exact phrase appears only here and in 1 Chronicles 29:10 in the Hebrew Bible. In the synagogue and the home it became the opening of every formal blessing, said over bread, wine, the Torah, the Shema and the weekday Amidah (the standing prayer). The Talmud discusses the form of such blessings (Berakhot 40b). Here, in the middle of a poem about being taught, the speaker blesses God and then asks to learn.

a: I will ponder your orders
p: Siach means to go over something in the mind or in speech. It is not the same verb as Psalm 1:2.
b: Psalm 1:2 uses hagah, "murmur" (see that note). Psalm 119 uses siach (119:15, 23, 27, 48, 78, 148) and its noun sichah (119:97, 99). Siach can mean to complain or talk at length (55:17; 77:3), and also to muse, to turn a matter over (77:12). The Plain renders it "ponder" all through this psalm. The Greek has adoleschēsō, "I will chatter, go on at length", which keeps the sense of words running on.

a: Uncover my eyes
p: A prayer for insight, said before reading Scripture in many churches and synagogues.
b: Gal is "uncover, take the veil off", the same root used for God revealing himself (1 Samuel 3:21). The speaker does not ask for a new law but for eyes to see what is already there. Christian readers set it beside the risen Jesus opening the disciples' minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45) and Paul's veil taken away (2 Corinthians 3:14–16). It is a common prayer before Bible study.

a: I am only a foreigner on the earth
p: A ger is a resident foreigner without land. One who does not know the country needs to be told the way.
b: The ger lived in Israel without land of his own and depended on others' goodwill (Leviticus 19:33–34). David's prayer says the same of all Israel: "we are foreigners before you, and lodgers, as all our fathers were" (1 Chronicles 29:15; compare Psalm 39:12). Here the point is practical: a foreigner does not know the roads, so he begs God not to hide the commands that show the way. The New Testament picks up the idea for believers as strangers on earth (Hebrews 11:13; 1 Peter 2:11).

a: the arrogant
p: The zedim appear six times. Scholars disagree on whether they are foreign rulers or fellow Jews.
b: Zedim, "the arrogant, the insolent", mock the speaker, smear him with lies, twist his case and dig pits for him (119:51, 69, 78, 85, 122). With them are "officials" (sarim, 119:23, 161) and "the wicked". Some scholars see Jews who had given up the law, perhaps in the struggles of the 300s or 200s BC over Greek ways (compare 1 Maccabees 1:11–15). Others see foreign powers and their local officers, as in Daniel. Others think the enemies are kept general on purpose so that anyone pressed for their faith can pray the psalm.

a: Officials sit and talk against me
t: Is the speaker a king or an official?
p: Officials plot, kings are faced (119:46). One scholar argues the speaker is the exiled king of Judah.
b: The speaker deals with sarim, officials or princes (119:23, 161), and expects to speak "in front of kings" (119:46). Will Soll argued that the psalm is a lament written for, or in the voice of, King Jehoiachin, the Davidic king held in Babylon (2 Kings 25:27–30), praying to be restored by keeping the law as Deuteronomy asks a king to do (Deuteronomy 17:18–19). Most scholars think the speaker is an ordinary devout Jew, perhaps a scribe or teacher, and that the court language is part of the picture of a righteous person under pressure.

a: My soul sticks to the dust
t: Sticking to the dust, sticking to God's decrees
p: Davaq, "stick, cling", comes twice in the dalet stanza: to the dust, and to God's decrees.
b: Lying in the dust is the posture of mourning and near-death (22:15; 44:25; Job 2:12). The speaker says his very self is glued to it. Six verses later he uses the same verb for his choice: "I stick to your decrees" (119:31). The stanza moves from being stuck in death to holding on to God's word. Nefesh, "soul", is the living self, breath and appetite (see the note at 19:7).

a: give me life
p: Chayyeni means "make me live". The KJV says "quicken me"; it is a prayer to be kept alive or revived.
b: The plea comes nine times (119:25, 37, 40, 88, 107, 149, 154, 156, 159), and the psalm says "your saying has given me life" (119:50) and that God's orders have (119:93). The Hebrew chayyah in the intensive form means "keep alive" or "bring back to life". The speaker is in real danger (119:87, 109) and also spiritually drained (119:25, 28). The KJV's "quicken" is old English for "make alive", as in "the quick and the dead". In the Plain the phrase is the same every time.

a: My soul drips away with grief
p: Dalaf means to drip or leak. Some Greek copies and the Latin took it as "my soul slumbered".
b: Dalaf is used of a leaking roof (Ecclesiastes 10:18) and of eyes dripping tears (Job 16:20). So the picture is either weeping or a life leaking away. The Greek manuscripts split: Rahlfs' text has estaxen, "dripped", which matches the Hebrew, while Codex Sinaiticus has enustaxen, "slumbered, nodded off" (both checked). The Gallican Latin dormitavit follows "slumbered". Later monastic writers applied the Latin to spiritual sloth (acedia, which is the very word both Greek texts use for "grief" here).

a: because you open my heart wide
p: A "wide heart" can mean understanding or freedom from pressure. Benedict quoted this verse.
b: In Hebrew a narrow place is distress and a wide one is relief (4:1; 18:19). "Widening the heart" can mean giving understanding (1 Kings 4:29 says God gave Solomon "breadth of heart") or giving joy and freedom (Isaiah 60:5). The speaker runs once God has made room in him. Near the end of the Prologue of his Rule, Benedict draws on this verse: as monks go forward in faith, their hearts are widened and they run the way of God's commands.

a: to the last
t: To the end, or as a reward?
p: 'Eqev can mean "to the end" or "as a reward". The same word ends 119:112.
b: 'Eqev is literally "heel", the back end of something, and so "to the end". It also means "result, reward", as in 19:11, where the one who keeps God's law gains much 'eqev. The Greek took it so in 119:112 (Rahlfs' text: "for a reward"; Codex Sinaiticus adds "continually"). The Plain follows the usual sense, "to the last", in both verses.

a: the saying that is for those who fear you
t: A saying that leads to fear
p: The Hebrew is short: "which is for your fear". It may mean the promise to those who fear God, or a promise that makes people fear him.
b: The phrase 'asher leyir'atekha can mean "which belongs to those who fear you" (the promise given to the God-fearing) or "which leads to the fear of you" (so that people will hold God in awe when it comes true). The Greek reads "for your fear". The Plain takes the first sense; the second is equally possible. In this psalm 'imrah often means a promise (see the note at 119:9).

a: And let your acts of loyal love come to me
t: The waw stanza: every line starts with "and"
p: Few Hebrew words begin with waw, so the poet began each verse with "and".
b: Waw is the Hebrew word "and", joined to the front of a word. Almost no other words start with it, so every verse in 119:41–48 opens with "and". The Plain keeps "And" to show the letter. The stanza turns outward: an answer to the mocker (119:42), speech before kings (119:46), freedom of movement (119:45). "Loyal love" is hesed, here in the plural, "acts of loyal love".

a: a word to answer
p: The speaker will answer his mocker with a davar because he trusts God's davar.
b: The verse plays on davar: literally "and I will answer the one who taunts me a word, for I rely on your word." The speaker does not plan revenge; his reply to insult will be a word that rests on God's word. Compare 1 Peter 3:15, where believers are to be ready to give an answer to anyone who asks the reason for their hope.

a: with room to spare
p: Rechavah is open country. The law is pictured as freedom, not a fence.
b: Barechavah, "in the broad place", is the opposite of the narrow straits of trouble (18:19; 31:8; 118:5). The speaker can move about freely because he has searched out God's orders. Christian readers compare James's "law of freedom" (James 1:25; James 2:12), and Jewish readers a teaching added to Mishnah Avot (6:2): the only free person is the one who studies Torah, reading Exodus 32:16 "engraved" as "freedom".

a: And I will talk about your decrees in front of kings
t: The motto of the Augsburg Confession
p: The first printed edition of the Lutheran confession of 1530 carried this verse on its title page.
b: When the Lutheran princes and cities presented their confession to Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530, the first printed edition, published soon after the Diet (1530–1531), carried this verse on its title page: they would speak of God's decrees before kings and not be ashamed. In the psalm the speaker may be a courtier, an exile at a foreign court like Daniel, or anyone made to answer for faith before power (Matthew 10:18; Acts 26:1–2).

a: the ones I love
p: Verse 48 is longer than its neighbors. Some scholars think "which I love" was copied in from verse 47.
b: Most verses of the psalm have two lines; verse 48 has three, and its middle phrase "which I love" repeats the end of 119:47 word for word. Many commentators suspect a copyist's repetition and print the verse without it; the Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek all have it, so the Plain keeps it. Lifting the hands is the posture of prayer (28:2; 134:2). Lifting them "toward your commands" is unusual and may be a gesture of reverence toward the scroll, or simply of longing.

a: Songs, that is what your rules have been to me
p: Zemirot are songs. Jewish families still sing zemirot at the Sabbath table.
b: The speaker has made God's rules into songs, the way people learn by singing. Zemirot (from the verb behind mizmor, "psalm") is the name Jews give to the hymns sung at the Sabbath table. "The house where I live as a guest" is literally "the house of my sojournings": a whole lifetime seen as a stay away from home, as Jacob calls his years "wanderings" (Genesis 47:9). The Talmud records a rabbi who blamed David for calling the Torah "songs" here, as if it were something light (Sotah 35a).

a: My share is the LORD
p: The Levites had no land: the LORD was their share. The speaker claims the same.
b: When the land was divided, the priests and Levites got no portion, because, as the LORD told Aaron, "I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites" (Numbers 18:20). Psalms 16:5, 73:26 and 142:5 and Lamentations 3:24 take the phrase for anyone whose whole wealth is God. Some scholars think the speaker of Psalm 119 was a Levite or temple singer; most think the phrase had become a prayer for any devout person. Compare 119:111, where God's decrees are his "inheritance".

a: In the middle of the night I rise to give you thanks
p: The Talmud says David rose at midnight because of this verse. Monks rise for the night office.
b: The Talmud (Berakhot 3b) says a lyre hung over David's bed, and at midnight the north wind played it, so David got up and studied Torah until dawn, citing this verse. Jewish mystics later kept a midnight prayer of mourning for the temple, Tikkun Chatzot. Benedict cites this verse with 119:164 for the monks' night office and their seven day offices (Rule, chapter 16). See also 119:147–148 on prayer before dawn.

a: Good is what you have done for your servant
p: Five of the eight tet verses begin with tov, "good". The stanza is about good that comes through being brought low.
b: Tov, "good", is the most common Hebrew word starting with tet, and the poet uses it at the head of 119:65, 66, 68, 71 and 72. God is good and does good (119:68), it was good to be brought low (119:71), and the law is good, more than gold (119:72). The Plain keeps "Good" in front where English allows. "Your servant" (thirteen times in the psalm) is how a worshiper, a prophet or a king speaks of himself to God.

a: Good discernment
p: Ta'am is literally "taste", the sense that tells good food from bad.
b: Tuv ta'am is "goodness of taste": the ability to judge well, as the tongue judges food (Job 12:11). Abigail is praised for her ta'am, her good sense (1 Samuel 25:33). The speaker wants a trained judgment, not only rules.

a: Being brought low did me good
p: Verses 67, 71 and 75 say affliction taught the speaker. Jewish and Christian teachers built on this.
b: Three times the speaker says he was humbled ('anah) and learned from it: before, he wandered (119:67); being brought low taught him the rules (119:71); God was faithful in it (119:75). The rabbis spoke of "sufferings of love" (yissurin shel ahavah), troubles sent to someone God loves, and tested the idea hard (Berakhot 5a). Hebrews 12:10–11 says God disciplines his children for their good. Both traditions also warn against telling a sufferer his pain is deserved, as Job's friends did.

a: more than gold and silver by the thousand
p: The law outweighs wealth: compare 19:10 and Proverbs on wisdom.
b: The psalm compares God's word to wealth three times: better than all riches (119:14), than thousands of gold and silver pieces (119:72), than gold and refined gold (119:127). Psalm 19:10 says the same, and Proverbs says it of wisdom (Proverbs 3:14–15; Proverbs 8:10–11; Proverbs 16:16). In this psalm torah and wisdom are one thing.

a: Your own hands made me and shaped me
p: The yod stanza opens with yadekha, "your hands". The one who made me can teach me.
b: Job uses nearly the same words in protest: "Your hands molded me and made me" (Job 10:8); the exact pair of verbs, "made" and "shaped", is in Deuteronomy 32:6. Here they are a reason for hope: the potter who shaped me can give me understanding. "Shaped" (kun) means set firm, established, as in Deuteronomy 32:6. Creation and teaching belong together in this psalm (119:89–91).

a: they bent me crooked with a lie
p: 'Iwwet means to make crooked, to pervert a case. It is a legal word.
b: The verb is used for perverting justice (Job 8:3; Lamentations 3:36) and for bending what is straight (Ecclesiastes 1:15). The arrogant have twisted the speaker's case with false charges. This and 119:86 and 119:154 sound like a person accused in court.

a: My soul is spent with longing for your salvation
t: The kaf stanza: worn out with waiting
p: Kalah, "be used up", opens 119:81 and 82, and the stanza is the psalm's lowest point.
b: The stanza is the darkest in the psalm. Soul and eyes are spent with waiting (119:81–82), the speaker is like a blackened wineskin (119:83), his days are numbered (119:84), enemies dig pits (119:85) and almost finish him (119:87). It is a lament in miniature, yet every verse still holds on to God's word.

a: I am like a skin bottle in the smoke
p: Leather bottles hung up near the fire went black, dry and wrinkled.
b: Wine and water were kept in goatskins (Joshua 9:13). The Hebrew says only "like a skin in smoke"; a skin hung up in a house without a chimney would blacken and shrivel in the smoke. The speaker feels dried up and useless, perhaps aged before his time. Some think a skin was hung in smoke on purpose to cure it or to age wine, which would make the picture one of being tested. The Greek reads "in frost", and the Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran has a different second line (see the variants).

a: When will you bring my pursuers to judgment?
p: Here mishpat means a judgment against enemies, not a ruling to keep.
b: "When will you do judgment on my pursuers?" uses mishpat, the same word rendered "rulings" elsewhere, in the sense of a verdict carried out. The Plain says "judgment" here because "bring my pursuers to a ruling" would not be English. Asking how many days he has left is the lament's question (39:4; 90:12).

a: Forever, LORD, your word
p: Le'olam, "forever", opens the stanza. God's word stands as firm as the sky and the earth.
b: The stanza ties God's word to creation: it is set fast in the heavens (119:89), the earth stands (119:90), all things stand by his rulings and serve him (119:91). Psalm 19 puts the heavens and the law side by side in the same way. Isaiah 40:8 says the word of our God stands forever, and Jesus says his words will not pass away even when heaven and earth do (Matthew 24:35; 1 Peter 1:24–25).

a: Your faithfulness runs from generation to generation
t: Another verse without a law word
p: Verse 90 names God's faithfulness, not his law, unless 'emunah is counted as a law word.
b: This is one of the four verses with none of the eight words (see 119:3). Some think the poet counted "your faithfulness" ('emunatkha) as one more name for what God has said, since his commands are called "faithful" (119:86) and his decrees "faithfulness" (119:138).

a: for everything is your servant
p: Sky and earth "stand" like servants before their master, waiting on his rulings.
b: To "stand" before a king is to be his servant, ready for orders (1 Kings 10:8). Heaven and earth stand by God's rulings the way servants stand at court. The same God who gave Israel the law gave the world its order: Jeremiah 33:25 speaks of God's covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth. Many readers find here an early form of the idea of laws of nature.

a: Without your law as my delight
p: Sha'ashu'im, "delight, play", comes five times. Proverbs uses it of Wisdom playing before God.
b: The plural sha'ashu'im (119:24, 77, 92, 143, 174) is the joy of a child at play (Isaiah 11:8 uses the verb of a nursing child playing by a snake's hole). In Proverbs 8:30–31 Wisdom says she was God's delight day by day, playing before him. Here the law is the speaker's delight. Later Jewish writing made the link explicit: Ben Sira says Wisdom is "the book of the covenant of the Most High God, the law that Moses commanded" (Sirach 24:23), and the rabbis read Proverbs 8 as Torah speaking.

a: Everything complete, I have seen, comes to an end
p: Tikhlah, "completeness", occurs only here. The meaning is clear in outline, unclear in detail.
b: The word tikhlah appears nowhere else. It is related to kalah, "finish", and seems to mean "completeness, perfection". The speaker has seen that every finished thing has its limit; only God's command has no edge. Some take it as a wisdom saying like Ecclesiastes (Ecclesiastes 1:2–11). Others translate "to all my hopes I have seen an end". The Greek reads "I have seen the end of all completion", which supports the usual sense.

a: How I love your law!
p: The mem stanza opens with a cry of love. Love of the law is the psalm's heart.
b: The verb "love" comes eleven times with God's teaching as its object (119:47, 48, 97, 113, 119, 127, 140, 159, 163, 165, 167). Christian readers have sometimes set this against Paul's words on the law. Paul himself writes that the law is holy and that he delights in God's law in his inner self (Romans 7:12; Romans 7:22). Jewish readers see in the verse the meaning of a life given to Torah study.

a: your command makes me wise
p: Deuteronomy promised that keeping the law would make Israel wise in the eyes of the nations.
b: Moses told Israel that keeping the rules would show their wisdom to the peoples: "This great nation is surely a wise and understanding people!" (Deuteronomy 4:6). Psalm 119:98–100 claims the same: wiser than enemies, teachers and elders. The Hebrew has the plural "your commands" with a singular verb, and the Plain follows the verb.

a: More than all my teachers I have gained insight
p: Mikkol can mean "more than all" or "from all". The Mishnah reads it the second way.
b: The prefix mi- can compare ("more than") or mean "from". The psalm means "more than", as in 119:98 and 119:100. But Ben Zoma in the Mishnah asks, "Who is wise? The one who learns from every person," and quotes this verse as "From all my teachers I have gained understanding" (Mishnah Avot 4:1). The two readings teach different virtues: confidence in God's word, and humility before every teacher.

a: More than old men I understand
p: Age was supposed to bring wisdom. The law brings more.
b: Elihu says the same against Job's friends: "Those with many years are not the wise ones" (Job 32:9). The speaker is not boasting of his own mind; his understanding comes from guarding God's orders. Compare Paul telling Timothy not to let anyone despise his youth (1 Timothy 4:12).

a: How smooth your saying is to my palate
p: Nimlats is "smooth, pleasant" to the taste. Compare 19:10 and the honey custom.
b: The verb is found only here; it seems to mean "be smooth, slip down easily". The picture of God's word as honey is in 19:10 (see the note there on the custom of honey on a child's first Hebrew letters) and Ezekiel 3:3. The Hebrew has the singular "your saying" with a plural verb, and the Greek and Latin read "your sayings".

a: A lamp for my foot is your word
t: A lamp for the next step
p: An oil lamp lit a few feet of path. The picture is guidance step by step.
b: A clay oil lamp gave a small light, enough to see where to put one's foot on a dark path, not to see far ahead. Proverbs 6:23 uses the same pair: "A command is a lamp, teaching is light". The nun stanza opens with ner, "lamp". Codex Sinaiticus reads "your law" here, while Rahlfs' text has "your word" with the Hebrew (see the variant). This is the best-known verse of the psalm and a favorite inscription on Bibles and church buildings.

a: I have sworn, and I will make it stand
t: A sworn promise to keep the law
p: The speaker has taken an oath to keep the rulings, as the returned exiles did under Nehemiah.
b: In Nehemiah 10:29 the people "take on themselves a curse and an oath: to walk by God's law". The speaker makes the same kind of vow for himself. Qiyyem means to confirm and to carry out: he will make his oath stand.

a: the freewill offerings of my mouth
p: A nedavah is a gift brought to the altar of one's own free will. Here it is a gift of words.
b: Freewill offerings were sacrifices no law required (Leviticus 7:16; Deuteronomy 16:10). The speaker offers words of praise instead, the way Hosea 14:2 speaks of offering "the bulls of our lips" and Hebrews 13:15 of "the fruit of lips". Some scholars think the speaker was far from the temple or wrote when prayer was taking the place of sacrifice for many Jews in the dispersion.

a: My life is in my palm all the time
p: "To put one's life in one's palm" means to risk it. The speaker lives in constant danger.
b: The idiom is used of Jephthah and David risking their lives (Judges 12:3; 1 Samuel 19:5; 1 Samuel 28:21). Something held in the open hand can easily be dropped or snatched. Codex Sinaiticus reads "in your hands", turning danger into trust, but Rahlfs' Greek text has "my hands" with the Hebrew (see the variant).

a: my inheritance
t: An inheritance that is not land
p: Nachalah usually means family land. The speaker's inheritance is God's decrees.
b: Every Israelite family had its nachalah, its land from the fathers (1 Kings 21:3). The speaker says God's decrees are his inheritance forever. Together with "My share is the LORD" (119:57), it suggests someone for whom the law has taken the place of land, perhaps in exile or under foreign rule.

a: People of divided mind
p: Se'afim are people split between two ways, like Elijah's hearers "limping" between the LORD and Baal.
b: The word is related to se'ippim, "divided opinions", in Elijah's challenge: "How long will you limp along on two crutches?" (1 Kings 18:21). The KJV "vain thoughts" follows a different guess. James 1:8 speaks of the "double-souled" man. The speaker loves a whole law and hates divided loyalty.

a: Turn aside from me, you who do evil
t: The only verse spoken to people
p: From verse 4 to the end the psalm speaks to God. Here alone the speaker turns to his enemies.
b: After the opening blessings (119:1–3), every verse addresses God as "you", except this one, where the speaker tells evildoers to get away so he can keep God's commands. Psalm 6:8 has the same cry, which Jesus uses in Matthew 7:23. It is also the only verse that calls God "my God" ('elohai).

a: Like slag you put an end to all the wicked of the earth
p: Sigim is the scum left when silver is refined. The wicked are what God skims off.
b: When silver ore is melted, the impurities rise and are thrown away (Proverbs 25:4). The prophets used the picture for God purifying his people (Isaiah 1:22–25; Ezekiel 22:18–22; Malachi 3:2–3). Here the wicked of the whole earth are the slag. The Greek reads "I counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors"; it may have read a different verb.

a: My body bristles with dread of you
p: Samar is the bristling of hair or skin in fear, as in Job 4:15.
b: In Job 4:15 the same verb is used when a spirit passes Eliphaz's face: "the hair of my skin bristled". Here fear of God makes the speaker's flesh creep. The Greek read the word as a command, "nail down my flesh with fear of you", and the Latin confige timore tuo carnes meas led Augustine and others to read the verse of the cross and of self-denial (Galatians 5:24).

a: Justice and righteousness are what I have done
p: Mishpat utsedaqah is the Bible's pair for social justice. Here mishpat is not "a ruling".
b: "Doing justice and righteousness" is what God asks of Abraham's family and of kings (Genesis 18:19; 2 Samuel 8:15; Jeremiah 22:15). The Plain says "justice" here, not "rulings", because the phrase is fixed. The ayin stanza opens with 'asiti, "I have done".

a: Stand surety for your servant
p: 'Arav is to stand guarantor for someone's debt. This is the verse with no word for God's teaching.
b: A guarantor pledged himself for another's debt or safety: Judah did it for Benjamin (Genesis 43:9), and Proverbs warns against doing it lightly (Proverbs 6:1). Job and Hezekiah ask God himself to be their pledge (Job 17:3; Isaiah 38:14). Hebrews 7:22 calls Jesus the guarantor (engyos) of a better covenant, and Christian readers linked this verse to it. It is the one verse in the psalm with no law word of any kind (see 119:3).

a: It is time to act for the LORD
t: Time for the LORD to act, or time to act for him?
p: The Hebrew can mean the LORD should act, or that people must act for his sake. The rabbis used the second.
b: 'Et la'asot laYHWH is "a time to act for the LORD". Most translations read it as a call on God to step in, because people have voided his law. The Mishnah reads it as a call to people: when the law is being broken, one may do something unusual for God's sake, such as greeting a person with God's name (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5). The Talmud uses the verse to explain why the oral law, meant to be passed on by mouth, was finally written down (Gittin 60a; Temurah 14b). The Plain's wording allows both readings.

a: all your orders about everything
p: The Hebrew reads "all the orders of all". Many scholars correct it to "all your orders".
b: The Masoretic Text has kol-piqqudei khol, "all orders of everything", an odd phrase. The Greek reads "all your commandments", which suggests a Hebrew piqqudekha, "your orders", and many scholars follow it. The Plain keeps the Hebrew and makes "about everything" part of the sense. See the variant.

a: The doorway of your words lets in light
t: An opening that lets in light
p: Petach is a doorway or opening. The verse may mean the opening up of God's words in teaching.
b: Petach is the ordinary word for a doorway (Genesis 18:1). Some read it as "the entrance of your words": when God's words come in, they bring light. Others take it as "the unfolding" of the words, their explanation, which is what a teacher does for the "simple" (peta'yim), the young and untrained (19:7; Proverbs 1:4). The Greek has "the revelation of your words".

a: as is right for those who love your name
p: Here mishpat means "the custom, what is right", not a ruling to be kept.
b: Kemishpat means "according to the custom" (Genesis 40:13; 1 Samuel 27:11): God's usual way with those who love his name. Because the word is not used for God's teaching here, some count 119:132 among the verses without a law word (see 119:3). The Greek reads "according to the judgment of those who love your name".

a: Shine your face on your servant
p: The words come from the blessing of Aaron in Numbers 6:25.
b: The priests blessed Israel: "May the LORD make his face shine toward you and be gracious to you" (Numbers 6:25). The psalms turn the blessing into a prayer (31:16; 67:1; 80:3). A shining face is a smile of favor, the opposite of a face hidden in anger.

a: My eyes pour down channels of water
p: The speaker weeps not for his own pain but because people do not keep God's law.
b: Jeremiah wishes his eyes were a fountain to weep for his people (Jeremiah 9:1), and Lamentations 3:48 speaks of eyes running with streams of water. Jesus weeps over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). The pe stanza ends with grief for others; the next begins with God's righteousness.

a: My zeal has been the end of me
p: Qin'ah is jealous passion for God. Compare 69:9, "Zeal for your house has eaten me up".
b: The speaker's zeal for God's honor consumes him because his enemies forget God's words. Psalm 69:9 says "Zeal for your house has eaten me up", which John 2:17 applies to Jesus. Elijah says "I have burned with zeal for the LORD" (1 Kings 19:10). The Greek translators heard Psalm 69 here too: Rahlfs' text reads "zeal for your house has consumed me", importing 69:9, while Codex Sinaiticus has "your zeal" (both checked; see the variant).

a: Your saying is refined all the way through
p: Tsaruf is metal refined in fire. Psalms 12:6 and 18:30 say the same of God's words.
b: "The LORD's sayings are sayings without impurity, / silver smelted in a crucible" (12:6), and "The LORD's word is refined like metal" (18:30). God's saying has been through the fire and nothing false remains, so the servant can love it. Proverbs 30:5 says the same.

a: and truth is what your law is
p: 'Emet comes in 119:142, 151 and 160. Jesus prays "Your word is the truth" in John 17:17.
b: 'Emet means what is reliable and lasting, not only what is factually correct. The law is truth (119:142), the commands are truth (119:151), the sum of the word is truth (119:160). Jesus' prayer for his disciples, "Make them holy in the truth. Your word is the truth" (John 17:17), echoes the line.

a: I am up ahead of the dawn
t: Ahead of the dawn, ahead of the night watches
p: Qiddamti and qiddemu, "I was ahead" and "my eyes were ahead", open the qof stanza's 147 and 148.
b: The speaker gets up before the light and his eyes open before the watchman calls the next watch. Neshef means twilight, and can be evening (Proverbs 7:9) or the dark before morning (Job 7:4); here it is the early morning. The two verses together picture prayer that starts before the day does.

a: the night watches
p: Israel divided the night into three watches, the Romans into four.
b: The Old Testament speaks of a beginning, a middle and a morning watch (Judges 7:19; Exodus 14:24; Lamentations 2:19). The Gospels use the Roman four (Mark 6:48). Monks later fitted their night office to these hours.

a: Those who chase after vile plans have come close
p: The qof stanza plays on "near": the wicked are near me and far from your law, but you are near.
b: Qarevu, "they have come close", is answered by qarov, "near", in 119:151: the persecutors are near, but the LORD is nearer. Compare 34:18 and 145:18. "Vile plans" (zimmah) is a word for scheming and lewdness. The Greek, and some Hebrew manuscripts as reported, read "my pursuers" (see the variant).

a: See my misery and rescue me
p: Re'eh, "see", opens 119:153 and 159, and 158 begins "I have watched".
b: The resh stanza begins three verses with the verb "see" (ra'ah): God is asked to see the speaker's misery (119:153) and his love for the orders (119:159), and the speaker has seen the traitors (119:158). The stanza is full of law-court words: plead, case, redeem (119:154).

a: Take up my case and buy me back
p: Rivah rivi is "argue my lawsuit"; ge'aleni is "redeem me", the act of a family redeemer.
b: The speaker asks God to be his lawyer in court (riv, a legal case) and his go'el, the relative who buys back a family member sold into debt or defends his rights (Leviticus 25:25; Ruth 4:4). Proverbs 23:10–11 says of orphans' fields: "their redeemer is strong. / He will fight their court case against you". Compare Job 19:25 and Jeremiah 50:34.

a: Truth is the whole of your word
p: Rosh is "head": the sum of all, or the first. The Greek says "the beginning of your words is truth".
b: Rosh devarkha 'emet can mean "the sum (total) of your word is truth", as rosh is used for a census total (Exodus 30:12), or "the beginning of your word is truth", as the Greek reads. The Plain takes "the whole".

a: Officials have hunted me without cause
p: Chinnam, "for nothing", is the word of 35:7, 35:19 and 69:4, which Jesus cites in John 15:25.
b: The speaker is hunted by officials (see 119:23) for no reason. "Without cause" is the complaint of 35:19 and 69:4, which Jesus applies to himself: "They hated me for no reason" (John 15:25). Yet what the speaker fears is not the officials but God's word.

a: Seven times in a day I have praised you
p: Benedict built the monks' day of seven offices on this verse.
b: Seven is the number of fullness (Leviticus 26:18; Proverbs 24:16). Benedict's Rule (chapter 16) takes the verse literally: "Seven times a day I have praised you" gives the seven day offices (Lauds, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, Compline), and 119:62 the night office. The Eastern churches keep a similar cycle of hours. Jewish prayer keeps three daily services (55:17; Daniel 6:10).

a: there is no stumbling block for them
p: Mikhshol is something you stumble over. Those who love the law walk securely.
b: Great peace (shalom, wholeness and safety) belongs to those who love the law, and nothing trips them. Isaiah warns of the LORD as a stone that makes the disobedient stumble (Isaiah 8:14), and 1 John 2:10 says the one who loves his brother has no cause of stumbling in him.

a: every way I take lies open before you
p: The shin stanza ends with the speaker's whole life open to God's view.
b: "All my ways are before you" means God sees everything he does (139:3; Proverbs 5:21). It is the ground for his confidence that he has kept the orders and decrees, and the reason he can ask God to judge.

a: Let my tongue sing back your saying
p: 'Anah is "answer", and also to sing in response, as choirs answer each other.
b: The verb 'anah is used for singing back and forth (Exodus 15:21; 1 Samuel 18:7; Ezra 3:11). The speaker's tongue will answer God's saying with song. The tav stanza is full of wishes: may my cry come near (119:169), my plea come in (119:170), my lips pour out praise (119:171).

a: I have wandered like a sheep that is lost
p: The longest psalm about keeping the law ends not in triumph but with a lost sheep asking to be found.
b: After 175 verses of love for God's law, the speaker ends by confessing that he has wandered and asking God to come looking for him. Readers have found this either honest humility, since even the law-lover needs God's seeking, or the voice of the exile, lost from home. The picture is the shepherd's (23:1–3; Ezekiel 34:11–16), and Christian readers hear Isaiah 53:6 and the parable of the lost sheep (Luke 15:3–7). Church fathers read it of Christ the good shepherd, who comes looking for the lost (John 10:11).

a: come looking for your servant
p: My own reading: the psalm is framed so that its speaker never claims to be one of the blameless of verse 1.
b: This is my own suggestion, not a standard reading, though many commentators note the humble ending. Verse 1 blesses "the blameless" (temimei), and verse 80 only prays "make my heart blameless". Meanwhile the verb "stray, wander" keeps returning: "keep me from wandering" (119:10), "those who drift away" (119:21), "I used to wander off" (119:67), "everyone who wanders from your rules" (119:118), most of them the verbs shagah and shagag. Two verses use ta'ah, and in the same form: "from your orders I did not wander" (lo ta'iti, 119:110) becomes "I have wandered like a sheep" (ta'iti, 119:176). The poem may be built to move its reader from admiring the blameless to admitting that the one who loves the law most is still a sheep that needs seeking.
